analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare offer its own prescription drug plan and negotiate drug prices directly with manufacturers.
analysis.headline: Introduced with six cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer at least one Medicare-run prescription drug plan, available nationwide starting in 2012, alongside the private Part D plans. Under this public option, the government would negotiate purchase prices directly with drug manufacturers, the way other federal purchasers do. It would also have created a streamlined appeals process for beneficiaries denied coverage of a drug.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — seniors and people with disabilities who buy Part D drug coverage. They would gain a government-run plan option with a single nationwide premium set at the plan's average cost, prices negotiated by Medicare itself rather than by private insurers, and a defined appeals process with independent external review when a needed drug is denied.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Health and Human Services to offer one or more Medicare-operated prescription drug plans with a nationwide service area beginning in 2012, giving beneficiaries a public alternative to private Part D plans.

Requires Medicare to negotiate the purchase price of covered drugs directly with pharmaceutical manufacturers and to use strategies similar to other federal purchasers of prescription drugs, such as a value-based formulary, to lower costs.
Sets a single, uniform national premium for the public plan based on its average per-person cost, so enrollees anywhere in the country would pay the same rate.

Creates a defined appeals process for denials under the public plan, including an initial review by the Secretary and an outside, independent review for denied appeals, so beneficiaries can get non-formulary drugs when medically necessary.

Builds the public plan's formulary around independent clinical evidence — the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality would assess which drugs give the most benefit for the cost, and a nine-member advisory committee of physicians, pharmacists, and consumer representatives would review manufacturer petitions under strict conflict-of-interest rules.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, which would face government negotiation driving down the prices Medicare pays for the public plan's drugs, and private Part D insurance companies, which would have to compete for enrollees against a Medicare-run plan. Because the public plan's premium must cover its full actuarial cost including administration, taxpayers would not be on the hook for its operating costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: The public plan would restrict access to some drugs: the Secretary is directed to exclude drugs from the formulary that offer less clinical benefit than alternatives, and the plan may use tiered copayments, prior authorization, step therapy, and reference pricing — the same kinds of coverage limits beneficiaries dislike in private plans.

Savings were not guaranteed. The bill required the premium to cover the plan's full actuarial cost including administration, so if Medicare's negotiations did not produce large discounts, or if enrollment skewed toward patients with expensive drug needs, enrollees' premiums would rise to cover the gap rather than the government absorbing it.

A single nationwide government plan competing against dozens of private plans could draw a large share of the market, and opponents argued it could crowd out private plans and give one federal agency outsized power over which drugs are covered and at what price.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicare beneficiaries the potential benefit was substantial: a public plan with government-negotiated prices and a uniform national premium, backed by an evidence-based formulary and a real appeals process. The costs are real but bounded — some drugs would be restricted or excluded, and any failure of negotiation would show up in premiums, not federal deficits. The larger cost fell on drug manufacturers and private insurers, not on the public. The main honest weakness is that the bill's savings depended on how well Medicare negotiated, which no one could know in advance.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dick Durbin introduced the bill on March 10, 2011, joined by Senators Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Daniel Akaka of Hawaii; it was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Finance.
The bill attracted six cosponsors — five Democrats and one Independent — and no other action of any kind followed.
The Senate Finance Committee never scheduled a hearing or markup, and the full Senate never voted on it; the bill died in committee when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers and private Part D insurers are better off, because a Medicare-run plan with government-negotiated prices never advanced. Medicare beneficiaries gained nothing; they continued paying prices set through private insurers without direct government negotiation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Part D insurers

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-IL), bill sponsor, Senate Majority Whip
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor

for.name: Six senators (five Democrats and one Independent)

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee; the bill received no action for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it never left committee

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry (PhRMA)
against.what_they_did: Long opposed letting Medicare negotiate drug prices and government-run drug plan competition, which this bill would create

against.name: Private Medicare insurers (AHIP)
against.what_they_did: Long opposed a Medicare-run public drug plan that would compete with private Part D plans for enrollees

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely from the Democratic side — the sponsor and all six cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent — and because no vote was ever held, the record shows nothing about how the rest of the Senate, including Republicans and moderate Democrats, would have voted.

industries.note: The bill would have required Medicare to negotiate purchase prices directly with manufacturers for the public plan's drugs and to steer use toward lower-cost drugs with equal clinical benefit, cutting into drug company revenue. Beneficiaries' savings would come largely out of manufacturers' prices.

A Medicare-operated drug plan offered nationwide would have competed directly with private Part D plans for the same enrollment, threatening private insurers' role and premium revenue in a program where federal subsidies flow through them.
